transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-17 15:00 PT | Duration: ~52 mins | Attendees: Maya, Liam, Sara (Redwood); Priya, Alex, Samir, Leah (Atlas HT)

Summary: quick recap of last week's smoke test, focus this week on capacity planning for Dedicated, autoscaling policy options, and burst handling. Agreed to run longer soak + share spreadsheet and security notes.

[00:00] Maya (AE): hey everyone thanks for joining on time, we'll keep to the 45-60 minute window, quick agenda: benchmark recap, sizing, autoscale policy options, next steps.
[00:22] Priya (CTO): yeah thanks, we've got a hard deadline end of month to sign off capacity for pilot, so want to nail the numbers and the fallback plan.
[00:38] Liam (SE): great, quick context 
 last week's smoke showed sustainable 120 rps at p95 latency 280ms on the 13B quantized variant, but we saw spikes up to 340 rps for short bursts which pushed latency to 700ms and some 502s.
[01:05] Alex (ML Eng): mhm, those 502s were during our daytime batch of bulk transforms 
 that was an unexpected tail. Could be KV cache miss pattern, we do a lot of session-switching.
[01:31] Samir (Infra): we also noticed the network egress pattern spiked 
 might be our VPC NAT gateway limits, not sure if it's Redwood or our infra.
[01:49] Maya (AE): good callouts. Today Liam will walk through suggested Dedicated sizing and autoscale configs, then we'll align on burst headroom and fallback to smaller models.
[02:08] Liam (SE): ok showing the sizing sheet we circulated 
 the 95th percentile steady-state is ~100-120 rps, but peak bursts can be 3x sustained for 30-120s. For Dedicated sizing we recommend baseline pool sized for 1.2x p95 (~145 rps) with autoscale policy to add burst nodes when short spikes > 150 rps for 60s.
[02:38] Leah (PM): can you clarify what you mean by "burst nodes" 
 are those different instance types or same pool with reserved burst?
[02:50] Liam (SE): good question 
 two approaches: 1) reserve burst capacity in the Dedicated pool (warm instances) that sit idle but are billed, or 2) configure autoscale with fast spin-up using a warm cache (we keep a small standby fraction with warmed kernels to reduce cold-start on spin-up). Option 2 reduces cost but can incur a 5-20s latency penalty on first requests during scale events unless we keep a warm fraction.
[03:19] Priya (CTO): cost matters for us; we can't have huge idle spend for months, but we also can't have user-facing timeouts. What are the typical cold-start times?
[03:31] Liam (SE): cold starts vary by hardware and model 
 on A100-class we see 10-25s to spin a new worker, on smaller GPUs maybe 20-45s; warming a subset lowers that to 1-5s. But note, with Redwood's warm kernel preloader and KV cache prewarming we can bring effective latency down. Also fallback routing to a smaller 7B variant gives sub-200ms latency with lower quality.
[04:05] Alex (ML Eng): that fallback sounds useful 
 we need to assess quality delta, though. For some prompts the 7B regresses too much. Could we do partial responses from 13B and then refill?
[04:19] Liam (SE): there are strategies 
 keep primary cached prefix on 13B then offload long-tail ops to 7B, but that complicates decoding and hallucination risk. Usually we recommend A/B test for quality tradeoff during pilot.
[04:41] Maya (AE): noted 
 we'll add a quality regression check tied to the eval set.
[04:53] Sara (CSM): quick operational note: per-route throttles and token quotas can help blunt a sudden noisy user causing burst. Do you currently have rate limits per API key?
[05:05] Samir (Infra): we do per-tenant rate limit at our proxy, yes, but some internal batch jobs bypass those rules today. We'll fix that.
[05:22] Liam (SE): back to autoscale policies 
 recommended config: target CPU/gpu utilization scaling with a minimum pool of 3 workers, max of 30, scale-out when 3-min moving average > 70% for 60s, scale-in when < 40% for 120s. Additionally add a burst policy: if instantaneous QPS > 2x baseline for >30s, spin a prewarm group of n nodes.
[05:55] Leah (PM): are those thresholds pre-tested? What about our SLO of p95 <= 350ms?
[06:05] Liam (SE): thresholds tuned from similar customers 
 meeting the p95 350ms SLO at peak requires both warm fraction and prefix KV cache hit rate > 80%. The sizing sheet models different KV hit assumptions.
[06:24] Alex (ML Eng): what KV cache hit rate did the smoke test show?
[06:29] Liam (SE): around 62% overall, but sessioned traffic had higher hits. Burst events dropped the effective hit far lower because new sessions don't have cached prefixes.
[06:44] Priya (CTO): can Redwood help with caching strategies at our app layer?
[06:51] Liam (SE): yes we have guidelines: sticky session tokenization, prefix caching for common prompts, and a client-side LRU for short-term reuse. We'll share the doc.
[07:03] Maya (AE): I'll add that link to the notes 
 link: https://redwood.example.com/sizing/atlas-poc-suggestions (note: placeholder link in transcript).
[07:15] [08:30] Speaker 1 (Customer): the team also wanted to confirm security needs 
 KMS for model keys and audit logs are must-haves before pilot.
[07:44] Maya (AE): yes, for Dedicated we support KMS/HSM integration and detailed audit logs; Sara will attach the SOC2 + architecture notes after the meeting.
[08:02] Sara (CSM): I'll drop the security summary and a network diagram showing VPC peering + NAT considerations. Expect that in the next 24 hours.
[08:14] Samir (Infra): thanks 
 that will help isolate whether some of the egress issues are ours.
[08:27] Liam (SE): back to sizing 
 we recommend two pools: primary high-capacity pool with 13B quantized for quality, and a low-latency backup pool with a smaller variant for overflow routing. Pool routing rules: route by weight+latency policy, with automatic fallback when primary p95 > 600ms or failure rate > 1%.
[08:55] Leah (PM): what's the billing implication of two pools? Is it double cost?
[09:03] Maya (AE): billing is per-worker-hour consumed; standby warm nodes count. If you use overflow routing to a hosted fallback instead of maintaining a second full pool in Dedicated, cost could be lower but raises data residency concerns. We'll include cost modeling in the spreadsheet.
[09:28] Alex (ML Eng): related to data residency 
 we need to ensure model tokens don't leave our VPC for hosted fallback. That's a blocker for some enterprise customers.
[09:41] Maya (AE): understood; we'll mark that constraint in the spreadsheet. For pilot we can keep all in Dedicated to avoid that issue.
[09:54] [10:10] Priya (CTO): ok let's talk about concrete numbers 
 if our peak day seen was 340 rps for 2 minutes, what pool size is that?
[10:22] Liam (SE): roughly each worker handles ~20 rps at our target latency for 13B quantized on the cluster type we tested. So 340 rps -> 17 workers. For headroom we recommend 25 workers to absorb 1.5x bursts and provide buffer for spin-up. That maps to baseline min 10, desired steady 14-18, max 30.
[10:50] Samir (Infra): do you have an estimate of tokens/sec or token cost at that scale?
[10:56] Maya (AE): we'll include token burn estimates in the pricing sheet; preliminary calc: at 340 rps with mean 120 tokens per call that's ~4.9M tokens/hour. We'll also show cost difference between quantized 13B and 7B fallback.
[11:17] Alex (ML Eng): one more question on autoscaling cooldowns 
 if we scale in aggressively we might evict cache and cause a cascading scale-up. How do you prevent oscillation?
[11:30] Liam (SE): use longer scale-in windows, circuit-breaker thresholds, and prefer warm-down to 60% rather than tearing down to min. Also keep a small warm fraction of say 10% to hold cache hot during scale-in. The sheet includes recommended hysteresis.
[11:53] Leah (PM): would it be possible to run a soak test that simulates our "morning batch + staggered user load" pattern?
[12:01] Maya (AE): yes that's exactly what we proposed 
 a 6-hour soak with periodic 2-minute bursts at 3x baseline every 30 minutes. Liam will run it and provide logs and dashboards.
[12:15] Liam (SE): plan: run soak in Redwood test cluster with matching model/quantization, mirror traffic shape provided by Atlas. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 latency, worker counts, KV cache hit rate, and failed requests.
[12:31] Priya (CTO): what telemetry format will you share? We prefer CSV and Grafana links.
[12:38] Liam (SE): we'll provide CSV + Grafana snapshot + raw logs behind S3 link.
[12:44] Samir (Infra): any requirement on our side to run the soak? e.g., firewall or whitelist IPs?
[12:51] Maya (AE): for Redwood-hosted soak we'll just need to whitelist the test runner IP if you want to hit a private endpoint; otherwise we can run in our isolated test environment and share results.
[13:05] Leah (PM): and timeline?
[13:09] Maya (AE): we can start the soak Friday 2026-11-20 and have preliminary results by Monday 2026-11-23. Follow-up sync Tuesday 2026-11-24.
[13:20] Priya (CTO): sounds good. Also please add the network diagram and KMS integration steps.
[13:27] Sara (CSM): will do.
[13:32] [14:00] Speaker 2 (Customer): minor 
 competitors were mentioned, do you have benchmark comparisons vs Anthropic?
[13:46] Liam (SE): we have public benchmark decks; quality and latency vary so it's more useful to compare on your eval set. We'll run the same eval across models if you'd like.
[13:58] Alex (ML Eng): yes please, run eval on our test prompts. We'll upload link to the shared drive.
[14:06] Maya (AE): action items recap: Liam runs soak by 11/20, Alex shares traffic histograms by 11/19, Maya will send sizing + pricing + security by 11/18. Schedule follow-up 11/24.
[14:28] Leah (PM): one last item 
 can we get an SLA summary for Dedicated? The pilot needs a preliminary SLO doc.
[14:36] Maya (AE): yes, I'll attach the SLA and we can align on pilot acceptance criteria 
 suggesting latency SLO p95 <= 350ms and error rate <0.5% for pilot sign-off.
[14:50] Priya (CTO): okay we'll review and come back. Thanks everyone.
[15:00] Maya (AE): thanks all, end of meeting.

References mentioned: sizing spreadsheet (shared), security summary & network diagram (to be shared), soak test logs (post-run).

Transcript notes: occasional mis-hears ("K-V cash" for KV cache), some speaker labels generic. This transcript is unedited and includes filler and overlapping talk typical of call exports.
